💡 Light and Shadow 101 - Part 2 (WHERE to place shadows and highlights) 💡  Do you struggle to understand WHERE to highlight and shade in your coloring pages? Then stick around because I will be breaking it down in a way that is easy to understand. Buckle up - this is a long one, but I am so confident this is the only video you will ever need to finally understand how light and shadow work.  And if stay to the end I will tell you where you can get this free practice worksheet (show worksheet) Also, make sure you press that plus button if you’re not already following to make sure you don’t miss the next 4 videos in this series.  With that, welcome to part 2 of Light and Shadow 101. My name is Stephie Colors, I hand illustrate coloring books, and in this 6 part series, I will be showing you how to add light and shadow into your coloring pages in a simple and non-complicated way.  Yesterday, we discussed why light and shadows are important for creating depth, dimension, form, contrast, mood, emotion, a focal point, and storytelling. Today we will be discussing WHERE to place your highlights and shadows. For this video, to keep it beginner friendly, we’ll be focusing on a single light source. Plus to be honest, I still struggle to fully understand multiple light sources. We will not be discussing cast shadows either just yet - that will be the last part of this series. The best way to teach you where to shade and highlight is with a demonstration - lucky for you I’ve done just that, so let’s check it out (swipe edit to demo with swoosh sound). I recommend for this part of the video that you clear your display. Hold your finger on the screen, then click clear display. Okay, so I’ve darkened the room the best I can to ensure there is only a single light source for this demonstration. I’ve also made sure there are no mirrors in this room to make sure no light is reflecting from anywhere either.  The simplest way to start understanding light and shadow is by observing it on a sphere, like this ball. The only ball I had in my house was a baseball - so I apologize if the red stitching makes it confusing. Let’s start with a light source coming from above.  The part of an object that is closest to the light will always be the brightest, and the part of the object that is farthest away from the light will be the darkest. (Pause on clip and circle the brightest point, the darkest) There usually is a highlight from surfaces that bounces back up at the darkest part as you can see here (pause and point an arrow)  but to keep this simple and easy to understand, we will not be focusing on that. In fact, ignore that completely. Watch as I move the light to the right and the left - the highlight and shadows move with it. If the light is to the right - that is where the highlight will be, and the shadow will always be to the left. If the light is to the left, the highlight will be to the left, and the shadow to the right. If the light is above, the highlight will be at the top, and the shadow to the bottom. Basically, the shadows will always be in the opposite direction of where the light is coming from. Now let’s practice this on the free worksheet you will be able to download at the end of this video! (Swipe transition with swoosh sound) The best way to start practicing light and shadow is by practicing in greyscale. I used to paint a lot, and when I was a teenager in private painting lessons, my teacher would not let me move on to using colors until I understood shading in black and white. For that reason, I’m going to demonstrate this using my grey markers, and I want you to practice the same way. In fact, a great way to start practicing light and shadow in your coloring pages would be doing a few monochrome pages.
